(9.6 / 10) Well worth the eight year wait - Author: archibalduk of EHM The Blue Line

More than eight years after the Eastside Hockey Manager series was put on indefinite hold, the undisputed king of ice hockey management is back. A lot has changed since EHM 2007 was released in September 2006; not least the rise of the likes of Steam and social media. These platforms make niche games cheaper to launch and easier to market. Indeed, Eastside Hockey Manager: Early Access (or EHM:EA for short) is being released exclusively on Steam and is likely to be heavily marketed using platforms such as Twitter and hockey forums such as The Blue Line and HFBoards. Against this background maybe, just maybe, the game will become a more viable project than it was before.

This new iteration is being released as an Early Access game. The game will be continuously developed over the coming months with regular updates being pushed to users via Steam. To call it a beta version would be grossly unfair and inaccurate. The game is highly polished. It’s simply that the game will be developed whilst we play. The thinking behind this approach is to test the waters. If the game generates enough sales then it will return as an annual release. If not, then it won’t.

Full Review -> http://gmgames.org/eastside-hockey-manager-early-access-ehm-ea/review/

After an 8-year hiatus, EHM makes its return via early access and while the game is very similar to its most recent iteration, that does not hinder or ruin the experience in any way.  As an early access game, this is a very polished and solid initial effort.

For those who haven't played EHM, the game is a text management sim where you take complete control of a team and attempt to use your skills as a general manager to take your team to glory.  As the game is in early access mode, there are no official licenses or real players.  However, www.ehmtheblueline.com has a very nice roster set, logos, and real team and competition names that provide that.  

Unlike NHL by EA Sports, you are the General Manager and do not control the players during games.  You sign free agents, hire coaches, scouts, and of course, trade as you desire.  Additionally, you can set your lines, practices, and tactics.  You also can promote and demote players between minor leagues and choose how to build your team.  As you're unable to control your players directly, tactics are very important in helping you win games.  The games themselves can be viewed via 2d mode where the players appear as dots with the puck, similar to the initial offerings of Football Manager 8 years ago, before it went 3D.  


The game engine is solid and provides a decent way to watch games and observe your players.  The minor gripe I do have with the game engine is that it does look dated especially compared with how SI has evolved its Football Manager franchise.  Having said that, the fact that this game was developed as a side project by SI mitigates that gripe somewhat.

The menus are cleaner than EHM 2007 although again, not as intuitive as the newest Football Manager games.  The other issue is that the game can only be run in one resolution which means that newer screen owners will not be able to view the game on a full screen.  Hopefully, that will be addressed in a future update.

If you love Football Manager, Out of the Park Baseball, and text sims, you owe yourself the privilege in checking this game out.  For $14,99, you simply can't go wrong.  The more people that purchase this game, the more likely we will see official licenses and future releases.  If you're an armchair hockey fan who thinks, sleeps, and drinks hockey, you definitely need to check this out.  Disappointed that your team continues to build around a questionable core?  Fix it yourself in EHM.  You won't regret it!

Eastside Hockey Manager, developed by Sports Interactive and available on Steam, is a deep and comprehensive simulation game that puts players in full control of managing a professional ice hockey team. For fans of the sport who relish the behind-the-scenes decision-making—from roster building and scouting to financial management and tactical planning—this title offers an unmatched level of depth. Though it lacks the glossy presentation and mass-market appeal of mainstream sports titles, it more than makes up for it with its authenticity and meticulous attention to detail. It’s a spiritual sibling to Football Manager, built around the same philosophy of realism and strategic control.

At its core, Eastside Hockey Manager allows players to take charge of nearly any professional or junior team from a wide range of leagues around the world, including the NHL, AHL, SHL, Liiga, KHL, and countless others. The breadth of leagues and player databases is staggering, and Sports Interactive has clearly made a concerted effort to reflect the real-world structures and dynamics of global hockey. Whether you're managing a perennial NHL contender or a small-market European team, the game adapts to your environment, with different rules, financial constraints, and player development paths. This global authenticity provides significant replay value, allowing players to test their managerial skills in vastly different hockey cultures.

Gameplay is structured around daily team management tasks. You’ll be handling contract negotiations, training schedules, scouting reports, player morale, and even media interactions. The game features an in-depth scouting system that mimics real-world evaluation techniques, including tracking player potential, mental attributes, and developmental ceilings over time. Drafting young prospects and nurturing them into first-line stars years down the line is one of the most rewarding aspects of the game. It requires patience, long-term vision, and strategic roster balancing, especially under salary cap constraints or when dealing with injuries to key players. The level of micromanagement can be overwhelming for newcomers, but for experienced sim players, it's a dream come true.

The tactical aspect of Eastside Hockey Manager is equally complex. You're not just setting lines—you’re building chemistry, creating power play and penalty kill strategies, deciding on forechecking intensity, and adapting your style to your roster’s strengths. Matches can be simulated quickly or watched play-by-play, with commentary that reflects real-time decisions and player performances. While the in-game visuals are limited to 2D representations and text-based feedback, they provide enough context to understand what’s working and what’s failing. The tactical feedback loop is robust, with detailed statistics, form trends, and opposition analysis allowing you to refine your approach game by game.

Visually, the game is utilitarian. The interface is dense and packed with data, with hundreds of screens dedicated to stats, reports, and rosters. While it can feel dated and intimidating at first glance, the design favors function over flair. Once you're familiar with the layout, navigation becomes second nature, and the sheer amount of available information becomes one of the game’s greatest strengths. However, this no-frills presentation may deter casual players or those expecting a more dynamic graphical interface. Still, for the hardcore hockey strategist, the spreadsheets and data tables are part of the appeal.

One of the standout aspects of Eastside Hockey Manager is its community and modding support. The game’s built-in database is already extensive, but player-made updates, real-world rosters, and even custom leagues add tremendous value. The user-driven updates help keep the game relevant long after official patches slow down. Community forums are active, offering advice, guides, and tools that help new players overcome the steep learning curve. Whether you're adding junior leagues, tweaking league rules, or importing historical data, the modding flexibility opens up near-limitless possibilities for long-term play.

That said, Eastside Hockey Manager is not without shortcomings. Its learning curve is steep, and the game does little hand-holding for newcomers. Tutorials are limited, and much of your early experience will involve trial and error. The lack of dynamic media narratives, visual flair, or player personalities—features that titles like Football Manager have increasingly embraced—can make some seasons feel clinical or detached. Additionally, the game occasionally suffers from user interface lag or minor bugs, especially when managing large databases or simulating multiple leagues.

Despite these limitations, Eastside Hockey Manager remains the definitive experience for players who want total control over a hockey franchise. Its unmatched realism, strategic complexity, and deep customization tools offer a uniquely satisfying simulation experience. It demands time, attention, and a love for the minutiae of the sport, but rewards that investment with a gameplay loop that feels endlessly rich. For hockey fans looking for a cerebral, spreadsheet-driven experience rather than arcade thrills or quick wins, Eastside Hockey Manager is not just a game—it’s a long-term project that captures the soul of managing a team in one of the world’s most dynamic sports.

This isn’t just a game — it’s an experience

Hours played: 1277 (and I’m still standing in the main menu listening to the music)

I don’t even know where to begin. It’s rare that something hits every single note — story, music, gameplay, visuals, writing — and does it so perfectly that you forget you’re staring at pixels. This game didn’t just entertain me; it ruined other games for me.

The story starts small. Just you, a broken world, and a reason to keep going — and before you know it, you’re caught in a web of choices that actually matter. The characters feel alive in a way that makes you miss them when you’re not playing. Every line of dialogue sounds like it was written by someone who’s lived a hundred lifetimes.

The soundtrack deserves its own review. Every note sinks into your soul. One minute you’re holding your breath through a quiet piano track, the next your heart’s pounding with orchestral chaos during a boss fight that feels more like a dance than a battle. I’ve had the title theme stuck in my head for days — and I’m not complaining.

Visually, it’s breathtaking. The world isn’t just beautiful; it feels lived in. Every light flicker, every distant echo, every reflection in the rain — it all tells a story. I took so many screenshots that I filled an entire folder called “emotional damage.”

And the gameplay? Smooth. Satisfying. Everything just works. It doesn’t hold your hand, but it never feels unfair. Every mechanic feels handcrafted to serve the narrative. Even the smallest side quests feel like pieces of a larger puzzle that rewards curiosity and empathy.

The ending… I’m still recovering. I sat there through the credits, controller in hand, watching the names of people who just changed my definition of what a “game” can be. Then I started New Game+ immediately because I wasn’t ready to let go.

I laughed, I cried, I questioned my life choices. And somewhere in between, I realized this isn’t a story about the player — it’s a story for the player.

EHM has really evolved since the old days. I last played it in the early-mid 2000s and was only marginally impressed. At the time my impression was "ok, this is nice but not what I'm looking for."

Fast forward some 15 or so years: WOW - the game is like night and day different! Loads of fun and very realistic. Taking it to the next level by bringing in Sega was a very smart move. Bringing more of the Football Manager element that allows for multi-player and really solid tactical customization right down to the individual player level brings about a level of hockey not seen elsewhere on the market. I like the fact that the styles of play can be customized to simulate anything from today's more "sanitized" NHL to the classic "old-time" hockey of the 70s, 80s and early 90s when brawls were common. By increasing player aggressiveness and selecting "encourage" as the fighting selection, I have seen some games that much more closely resembled the rough and tumble, bump and shove, drop the gloves hockey I grew up with 40-50 years ago. That level of customization - plus all the great mods that are available for rosters, logos, face packs, etc., make this the must-have hockey game for any serious PC sports gamer.

I'd love it if more classic seasons become available via the community. It would be a blast to play the Big Badd Bruins of the early 70s or the French Connection Habs of the late 70s or the Broad Street Bullies or Gretzky's high-flying Oilers. This game sets up perfectly for these kinds  of mods.

DISCLAIMER: I want to start out by noting a couple of things that may be relevant to people interesed in this game. First, I never played Football Manager in any form, nor did I play this game's old 2007 iteration. I had no biases coming into this game. Second, while I am a hockey fan (Go Bolts!) I was not a hardcore fan. I was (and largely am) still fairly casual in that I don't follow mundane stats, am not up to date on every player in the league and don't watch every single game. 

That being said. This game is fantastic! I am having loads of fun with this gaming experience and as far as I can tell will be having lots of fun for months if not years to come. 

Who would like this game? 
- anyone who enjoys management games
- anyone who enjoys stats and tactical games
- any sports fans (hockey is a plus!) 

PROS:
- addictive gameplay that makes you feel involved and responsible for your teams success and failure

I played Franchise Hockey Manager 2 (FHM2) for a while and then got Eastside after so this is a comparison between the 2.

Pros:
- New rosters available (if created by a modder). You dont have buy a new game to get new rosters.
- Ability to shop player (This is available in FHM4)
- You can decide what each player means to your orginization, like if he is a core piece or fringe player. You also get prompted with interviews or actions to take if a player has a bad stretch or whatever. These are pretty rare but kinda interesting
- In-game visuals are fun to watch sometimes and are very customizable. You can watch every second or none at all.
- Overall more enjoyable than FHM2

Cons:
- Less historic rosters than FHM2
- You will get a 'email' on basically anything that happens in that league and 85% are not relevent. I have not found a way to filter them
- The "player rating" feature isn't very useful. Basically any NHL player in the NHL will get rated 6-10. Obviously if you put a AHL player he will score lower. I wish it was based off of their skill level or contract size. If a top player in the leauge like Ovechkin doesn't do much, he should score worse than a 4th liner that has similar game stats.
- Each day is broken into 3 sections; morning, evening, night. This means there is 3 clicks and simulations that take place each day, and if it's after the trade deadline and all your guys are healthy you have to click a million times to sim to the end of the season. Not a big deal just annoying when there is little to do, and there is a lot of times when there is nothing to do.
- Player stats are sort of confusing. There are no defined offensive and defensive stats, which makes it hard to figure out who is a better player in a trade. Thinks like "Determination" and "Work Rate" and "Anticipation" are difficult because I don't know how important they are. Should an offensive player have a high Anticipation? Or is that a defensive trait? If a offensive player with a high Work Rate is rare, is he worth keeping? Is it more important than high wristshot or stickhandling?

Tl;dr - If you like up to date rosters and a new game (and possibly new features) every year or so, get the latest FHM game. If you just want to mess around with a cheap hockey manager game and have the ability for modders to make up-to-date rosters, get this game.

You probably already know if you want EHM or not. If you aren't a hockey fan, and if you don't like pretty deep simulation-based games, there's nothing for you here.
However, if you like those two things, EHM isn't perfect, but it is the best option in the genre. Sports Interactive know what they're doing, and EHM is no different, although it is a little barebones. It's a shame that, for what is ostensibly a new game, there's no modern features such as achievements. Thankfully it does have Workshop support, and it's here we see EHM's trump card.
EHM's modding community is what, for me, pushes the game from standard sports-sim to something engrossing. Real-world rosters and clubs, as well as facepacks, allow for something more realistic - and thus, fun. For me, trying to turn my beloved Calgary Flames from perennial bottom-feeders into an actual force is far more enjoyable than doing it with a fantasy club, with fake players. Without these mods, EHM is pretty sparse.
On its own, EHM is a tough sell. Even with it's fantastic mod support, it caters to a pretty small niche. If that niche includes you, though, you'll be treated to a game that demands time and patience, but yields great reward.

This is coming from the perspective of someone that played NHL GM Modes up to NHL 14. The games after that, except maybe for NHL 15 on the PS3 and X-Box 360 didn't improve anything in GM Mode, so I came in knowing the ins and outs of the GM Mode in the NHL games at their peak regarding simulation. This is also after one full season, so look at this reason.

As far as realism, I would say it is fairly decent, but obviously it cannot be 100% accurate, as it cannot always predict when players will have off or good seasons. In my season with the Kings, I made it into the finals in year one and faced the Tampa Bay Lightning. While initially unrealistic, Tampa didn't have Stamkos most of the year and almost made the playoffs, and in this game Kopitar and Gaborik had good years, as the Kings main problem was scoring, not allowing goals, even when Budaj was the starter. As for the simulation engine, the best testament to it's realism is being able to watch and coach the games. How you do this is your own choice. I believe you can have the games be coached by an AI, but that takes the fun out of the game in a way. And this indirectly leads to this game's double edged sword: time. While you become more accustomed to the day to day job of a general manager/coach, there is a heavy amount of time to be invested in a single season of this game. As I said earlier, I only played one full season (including the playoffs) and it took me over 20 hours. However, this one season was definitely fun as I got closer to the team and was satisfied with the simulation and the way stats worked for the most part, and the many coaching options the game gives you. The trading system is also very interesting as it allows you to offer a player to the league and see what offers teams give you. The spread of trade rumors also adds to the fun of the situation.

Another great thing about this game and being able to coach them and watch them, is the addition of the amount of personality that goes into this game. This was best characterized by a series I had with the San Jose Sharks. In I believe it was game 2 or 3, the Kings were pounding the Sharks, and I remember us having 7 goals or something crazy at the end of the game. After the first or second period, Drew Doughty was injured by a Sharks player and I went crazy and adjusted a lot of my players so that they could fight and have them target Sharks players like Couture and the guy that injured Drew, who seemed to be some nobody. At the beginning of the third, a line brawl broke out and even the goalies joined in, though this would cost Quick a suspension and the Sharks backup would get the suspension, not Jones as he was pulled. After the line brawl I'm not sure if a fight broke out in the game, but it was a crazy moment, one you literally cannot have in EA NHL GM Modes. Drew came back for the next game and we lost the next game, but it wasn't the fault of the goaltender as we didn't get enough done in regulation. In the end, we won the series in seven games. To me, this is what a rivalry series was supposed to feel like, crazy, intense, hard-fought, and brutal. This single series made me fall in love with the game.

So should you or should you not buy this game? While I've only played one season all the way, I definitely enjoyed that one season. I cannot accurately judge player growth as I haven't invested much time into the game. From what I experienced, if you're willing to invest time into this game and want a realistic hockey sim, go for it, this may be the best one out there, but I haven't played Franchise Hockey Manager 3 so I can't compare it to that game. If you're not patient enough to essentially "play" as the coach then this game may not be for you. 

One more thing, you need to download NHL rosters from the workshop if you want to use those.

tl;dr If you're willing to invest time into a realistic hockey sim, this game is for you as it adds a ton of personality to being a general manager. If you aren't patient enough, maybe manager games aren't for you.

I've been playing this series since EHM 2005, although it was EHM 2007 that I put in hundreds of hours.  This version of the game is an iterative improvement over EHM 2007.  It appears to be a conservative migration to SI's latest app engine, but maintains a very similar flow to EHM 2007, not the latest Football Manager game.

With that said, this game is simply spectacular.  I've only played a few games into my season with this version (so I'm not an authority on the state of completeness) but what I've seen so far is fantastic.  I've had some gripes with FHM 2007, fortunately it appears that quite a few of them have been addressed.  The fact that SI is bringing this game back is astonishing considering how they unceremoniously dropped the game after pirating concerns shortly after it was released in 2006.  Those of us with the Mac version really got screwed since there were some terrible bugs that were never fixed.

Regardless, I'm really excited for the future... If this game gets half the attention FM gets, we're in for a treat.  I have a feeling what we are playing now is a wait-and-see product- see what the respose is to this conservative effort and decide if it's worth investing any additional effort.  Judging from the response so far it should be a resounding YES, this game deserves 1st class attention!

Anyway, newcomers from FM are going to need to be patient, the UI is no where near as mature as FM.  FM has had the benefit of many years of iterrative development... while EHM has been in stasis for 8 years.  Even if this release just brings EHM up to date and nothing more, we all win.  Hopefully next years release will start incorporating some of FM's ground breaking systems.  

This game is worth every penny whether you are new to the series or upgrading from EHM 2007.  My favorite sports sim ever, hands down.

I played the two earlier versions of Eastside Hockey Manager back in the day, and the latest EHM project holds the same charm and appeal with more depth.

Unfortunately, despite the many similarities, EHM hasn't been given the same backing and resources as the great Football Manager series, mainly because ice hockey is a much more niche thing compared to football on a worldwide scale. Therefore EHM has not evolved to its full potential over the years. That is not to say it isn't a worthwhile hockey simulation and management experience, because it really is. It's just obvious it could be so much more developed as far as media and people interaction, training, player personalities, transfer speculations, diversity of many small detail and options, tactical consistency, the graphical game representation, scouting reports, tactical and personnel advise from your coaches etc. go, had it been brought forward through the FM path.

One of EHM's strengths is the wide array of leagues and teams at your disposal. The main focus is NHL, which means that the National Hockey League's trading, contracts, drafting, scouting etc. have been well implemented. If you're looking for a change, then the European leagues offer a freshly different experience; some have league tiers with promotion/relegation structures, and the trading/buying of players differs from that of the NHL franchise. When laying an NHL-based save, I felt the other countries' talented players were nicely included in the Northern America-focused database, and looking for new prospects - whether from overseas or the USA/CAN minors - felt like actually scouting for the National Hockey League.

I have to say the weakest part of EHM is the much dated match engine. In Football Manager I can actually use what I see unfolding in the match as legit info on what small changes to make, who is playing how, which opponent looks dangerous, which side looks like it could be exploited and so on. In EHM the little dots are often skating around much like figure skaters and it could be just my underdeveloped hockey brain, but I cannot make heads or tails of it. I cannot decipher what needs to be changed tactically, and keep getting frustrated by the lacklustre marking and movement of my defenders or the way my forwards - contrary to my advise - lose their man too easily, leave them open for easy goals at the near or far post and slash, hold, crosscheck, hook and trip themselves into the penalty box time and time again.
If only the match engine was remodeled so that it could present more useful and accurate information of the game being played, it would make the coaching so much more sensible.

All in all Eastside Hockey Manager is a very good hockey managing/coaching simulation that yet doesn't fully live up to its vast potential.

I'm giving this game a negative review despite loving it. The reason is that I want to draw attention to the negative sides that I don't feel get mentioned often enough.

First of all, there are still bugs in the game. After so many  itterations, one would have thought that things like trading and contracts would work flawlessly, but nope, you'll still run into situations where you need a save file editor or create another GM just to get the game to follow hockey rules.

My other and biggest issue is with the way this game compensates. Let me explain. I've been playing EHM since the very first version, probably spent thousands of hours on all versions together. One thing you have to realize is that this game is essentially a numbers generator, working with probability and such. Thing is, if you've been playing this game long enough, you'll find ways to build fantastic teams, with (probably)  the best coaching staff in NHL history and you can pretty much win the Stanley Cup with any team by your second, in a worst case scenario 3rd season. But! The game detects when your team or player start producing extraordinary numbers, and it will start compensating to keep things "realistic". Won too many Stanley cups in a row? Well, you'll lose in the playoffs, no matter what you do (tested by replaying the same saves when things got weird on countless occasions). You'll win with the same team next year, but the game won't let you win, say 4 times in a row, just because. Same if your team is scoring too much. Built a scoring machine with 1st line level players on your 3rd line? Well, bad luck, because you're gonna get punished by periods where your team will refuse to score, until your goals scored total returns to a "normal" value, then, without changing anything, you score again. Same goes with winning games. Winning 90% of your games mid season? Well, here's a drought, it'll end once you're around 75-80%, then you'll dominate again and the cycle repeats.

Bloody hell EHM, let me build super teams if I want to, don't punish me for finding ways to work the system. Sheesh! What's the point in learning to play a game if it will punish me for that and promote mediocrity?

Otherwise, I really enjoy this game and I value the work they put into it, it's a great game, but the compensation system can be incredibly irritating.

After several hours of playing Eastside Hockey Manager: Early Access Edition I can say that it is one of the most enjoyable and addictive simulation games I have ever played.  I always enjoyed various football (soccer for us in N. America) simulations but I love hockey and am so glad that a game developer has introduced (in this case re-introduced) a simulation for hockey fans.   

Pros: The game offers a variety of setting which allow you to establish how many hats you want to wear when managing the team you take over.  You can just manage (draft, develop prospects, sign free-agents, trade players, hire and fire coaches, scouts and other personnel, salary cap) while analyzing endless statistics or micro-manage every aspect of your team by adding coaching responsibilities to your portfolio and establish in-game tactics and select game-day rosters.  The game has an active modding community.  You can download NHL player rosters or other professional league players and team logos for a more realistic experience.

Cons:  
- The game could offer higher resolution settings than the 1024 x 768. 
-  Also while the lower resolution does not detract from game play I have found that when I quit a game the default      resolution setting on my Windows desktop sometimes reverts to the 1024 x 768 resolution setting that the game uses (from my normal desktop resolution of 1920x 1200). Not a big deal to change resolution back to 1920 x 1200 but a nuisance. 
- In rare instances some of the historical statistics do not tally correctly. 
-  Some statistics do not export correctly to a file or printer

Game Improvement:  
- I would like to see some graphical updates made to the game as some of the 2D graphics seem a little dated like when watching individual games.  
- Also would like to see when winning a cup or when a player I manage wins an individual trophy,  it would be nice to have a graphic of a newspaper where headlines highlight the achievement like I have seen in other sports sims.  

Recommendation:  The game for an early access product is well developed and if no further development of the game was offered would still represent extremely good value.  There are some small tweaks that need to be made with the game which is to be expected with an early access product.  With that said I can say without hesitation that if you enjoy sports simulation games, you will not regret purchasing this title.

From Version 15.0.1b (first early access version) here are some of my findings on the game:

Pro's: 
- Has nearly all the features from the EHM 2007, meaning it already is the deepest hockey sim available.
- Nice new touches like players bio information talking about players close friends on the team.
- Nice tactical improvements like individual strategies for players
-Tactical improvements for lines including choosing who would be the playmaker on the line.
- Free Agency is much more realistic. Don't expect to always build your teams on July 1st, UFA's want money and term just ilke in real life.
-Position's of players are more in-depth, including their roles like defensive defenseman, stay-at-home defensemen, 2-way forward, skilled forward, quick forward. This adds to the fun of building cohesive forward units.
-Tons of international tournaments, take control of your favorite national team and try to build a team to bring glory to your country.
-The in game match view has been improved and is very enjoyable watching your team battle it out.


Con's:
- Interface and menus are very similar to EHM 2007 so it is missing some more modern interface options.
- Resolution needs to be improved for modern pc's
- Scoring has to be balanced a bit more to 2015 scoring levels (its a bit too high at least in NHL games).
- Missing leagues like the Swiss leagues, Russian MHL, and British Hockey leagues from 2007 version.
- Coaches and GMs get fired a little more than in the real world.

There are a few issues like the small window the game runs in and the interface definitely needs some modern touches, but the rest of the cons are minor. The positives far outweigh the negatives with this release. Please do yourself a favor and buy this game if you enjoy the sport of hockey and have ever wanted to build your dream team or test your management skill in the lower leagues and build a legendary story as you climb the ranks to finally leading your national team to world glory.

I used to play the Madden and NHL series through PSX and PS2 when I was in Middle/High School, but after graduating from HS, I became much more of a PC gamer and stopped keeping up with the consoles.  As a result, I don't play many of the sports sim games, though I do get the urge to try one about once a year or so.  I'd heard good things about the Sports Interactive Manager series, and when they released a new version of Eastside Hockey Manager, I decided to give it a shot.  I was very impressed with how deep and involved the game is.  EHM gives a very realistic simulation of an NHL team, and you can control almost any facet of your team.  If you're not already aware, know that it is a simulator - you're not actually controlling players and scoring goals, if you choose to "watch" the games, you're watching little dots go around the rink to do their job.  It's an enjoyable experience to play through, especially as a second screen or casual sort of game while you're watching something else (playoff hockey?) on the other screen.  For what it is, EHM is a very solid simulator of the GM/coaching elements of a hockey team.  

EHM does have some interface and management elements that are unintuitive or cumbersome to manage.  Aside from that, for what it is, EHM is a very good sim - but it doesn't quite scratch the itch for a Madden or NHL type game that my friends and I used to spend weekends plowing through season after season.  It was an interesting experience and a good one (especially in the hockey world, where we have few enough options as it is), but it didn't satisfy the same way that throwing hits and scoring goals does in those more traditional sports simulators.

I don't usually write reviews, but this game is already so good and still has such great potential, coming from a die hard hockey fan, I love this game. 
Pros:
Scouting - Scouting mission details can be changed like player age, position, or ignore well known players/prospects, and it really helps you find the players you need, whether you're playing as Arizona stocking up on talent, or Detroit looking for a diamond in the rough, or Montreal and you are looking for some proven foreign skill to boulster your roster for the cup run, you can find the players you need. You can also generalize the scouting by assigning a scout to a continent, or country/nation, or you can assign him to individual leagues, you can even assign a scout to a particular player if you'd like.

Game simulation- You can choose to simply speed up games to get it over with, or you can watch the game real time and make tactical changes, line changes, etc. 

Line Changes/team tactics/unit tactics/player tactics- Wow. Just great. You can change defensive zone strategies, neutral zone defensive strategies/positioning, neutral zone offensive strategies/positioning, forecheck, breakout strategies, offensive zone strategies, and of course special team units like PP and PK. You can choose which player is le playmaker of the line, choose who takes faceoffs (which is great I'll explain further in), etc you have absolute control of your lines. You can also change individual tactics, so if you have two offensive players and a power forward on your first line, you can change the line to not body check often or hard, and not be aggressive, then go to your power forward individually and make him check hard, play aggressively and with a high tempo to balance out your line, or set a defensive type of player to shadow an opposing player and keep him in check.

You also have control over practice so you can train what coaches do what (coaches have attributes like coaching defensive players at 17/20, but then he might have 11/20 for coaching forwards and a poor goalie stat as well, so make him only handle defeinsive training. I believe it helps, clarification would be nice though. You can make certain player focus on an area of the game that maybe he is weak at, or boost what he's good at even more. You can have signing bonuses for games played, points, shut outs, etc.

Those are a few things that stuck out that I liked

Cons:

Now, I know you want it to be hardcore simulation, very in depth etc. But damn, it takes a looooong time to get through seasons. I want to go outside and do shit still, and have a life. I like it being in depth. Although I have quite a bit of time played, I find it extremely hard to get in to when it takes me like six hours or sometimes longer to finish the season. Just make an option to set a date a date simulate up to it. I know that's like EA NHL's simulaion, but it does work good. Or at least a quick sim game option. I know it might "dumb the game down" but the players that don't want it don't have to use it. Not everyone has time to play for six hours, although it's so good I have played for even longer in one session before. It may also interfere with game longevity, so I guess it's a choice the devs need to make. I really hope that isn't an option already that I haven't found lmao.

Player Overall and progression- (My only semi-major gripe about something wrong/broken with the game, not having quick sim is not wrong/broken, it's just not included)This is pretty simple to understand why it must change slightly... I will have great prospects for the future, but they are young and only really strong in the physical category on the far right like speed, strenghth etc. and since they are so strong in that category, they have a four star "current rating" so if he's playing in the AHL he will be unhappy because he's rated four stars, but then I call him up, and he's a complete liability on the ice, and he does poorly in the big league, and his potential may drop or he may not grow properly. The worst part is, if you don't call them up they will get unhappy and eventually request a trade and in some cases not resign a contract so you just lost out on a valuable draft pick simply because he was being a cocky bigot (imporper use of bigot ik) that thought he was the shit, then his hopes got crushed and blames it on me. Eastside Hockey Manager is easily the best hockey sim I've played.  The amount of options it gives you can sometimes be a bit overwhelming, especially if you like playing under the hood to find that perfect set up.  FAIR WARNING though:  options come at a price.  Not a monetary price, this game offers an extremely fair price for what it delivers.  I'm talking a learning curve price.  If you like sports sims , especially hockey sims, do yourself a favor and buy this game.  Then do yourself an even bigger favor and download the Users Manual:  

http://cdn.akamai.steamstatic.com/steam/apps/301120/manuals/2015_Game_Manual.pdf

Trust me on this - do it!   You're welcome.

By now, it is obvious, I like this game.  However, in the interest of fairness in my review, it does have a few warts.  The way screens are laid out stat-wise could be improved.  During a game, the Head Coach will sometimes change a tactic and it is nigh impossible to figure out what he is changing because nothing points it out to you.  Sometimes when you set the status of a player you are about to offer a contract to (in effect telling the player how much your team desires him:  "key player" "core player" "regular player" "hot prospect" etc), the player will refuse to listen to you because he wanted a higher status - but you frequently get no way to change the status you gave him.  I get an annoying error infrequently when reading my mail but it doesn't affect game play at all.

There are a few other minor quibbles, but that is exactly what they are:  minor quibbles.  Every game has a few and none in Eastside Hockey Manager are big enough to create caution or concern. 

Fantasy Draft?   check
I Do Everything GM Mode- Keep Your Filthy Hands Off My Team?  check.
I Just Want to Handle Trades and Financials - You Do the Rest?  check.
Minor Leagues?  check.
Foreign Leagues? check.
Gobs of stats? check.
Ability to set lines, team tactics, unit tactics, individual tactics, dictate who takes face-offs, who shoots in what order in shoot-outs, tell specific players they have a green light to pick fights, allow specific defnsemen to carry the puck and/or join the rush, and much more? check.
Realistic results? check.   (Caveat: some people think defensive players with offensive talents are a but short-changed in terms of goals/assists this version of the game.  My experience is I have had various offensive minded defensemen score between 60-80 points a season.  Perhap,s I am just adjusting their personal tactic settings to best suit their play.) 
Ability to customize to play how you personally want to play?  check.
Fun factor?  check.
Stable?  very.
Great graphics?  Come on - it's a sports management sim, what do you think you're gonna get?  The in game graphics are very easy to follow.

Bottom line?  BUY IT!

Despite the minimalistic animations of the game, which essentially consist of watching 10 dots with small sticks running around the ice,  the clear meat of the game is within the management aspect of the game, hence the title.

Players in EHM do not have a single 'overall' skill number and instead have over 25 different skills ranging from things like Slapshots, Flair, or Stamina. As well, the coaching staff, including physiotherapists are also ranked with a number of different skills.

Coaching - You can design a gameplan for your team down to the most minute detail. Different sliders for lines and d pairings. Or you can let the coach take over. 

Staff - You can also hire assistant coaches and head coaches with various skills as well as physio, assistant gms, and as mentioned above full teams of scouts. 

Trading - Trading is much more balanced than the NHL games. You can't really 'cheese' the draft system although you can definitely stockpile picks and make good trades thanks to good scouting. I found it relatively easy to build a dynasty in the game and that's a good thing IMO. IT's not as easy as it is in EA but that's also a very good thing imo. It's entirely possible to build a team with the best intentions, miss the playoffs repeatedly, miss your window, and be forced the rebuild. 

Development - Amazing development in this game. Your players development is dependent on a few things. How good is your coaching staff? How do they perform during the season? And also what practice routine do you set for them? Practice is a very fleshed out gameplay element that allows you to customize how you want your players to improve. It's a lightyear ahead of EA NHLs somewhat random system. Potential can change if a player has an amazing seaosn, improving, or get worse if you're playing the player at a level below their current skill (Like placing a NHL ready third line player int he AHL for example). 

Fantasy Draft - it has a fantasy draft with a lot of settings. 

Community - Amazing community that uploads roster updates for FREE EVERY YEAR. EA would charge you 80 dollars for what this community releases for free. 

Actual simulator: It's nothing special. Design is reminicsent of 'table hockey' you might play in a Canadian basement. You don't have to watch the games but I find watching them pretty entertaining. 

The balance - Balance of players and teams is very strong. it's hard ot win with one good line and three lines of plugs. It's hard to win without good goaltending. It's hard to win without defense. You can build a defense first team or a run and gun team. 

Overall: Recommend this as a must buy for fans of GM mode and NHL. There's nothing even close. I tried the older FHM but not the newer one.

I originally used to play a very large amount of the NHL series on my PS4, and while it was fun to occasionally hop in and actually play the game, I found myself just simming through the franchise mode, season after season to watch my players and team progress. Once I found EHM, I almost entirely stopped playing NHL on my PS4. I realize not everyone will be like this, but if you are a fan more so of the sim aspect of other hockey games, this game will be perfect for you.

EHM is very deep in comparison to the NHL games on console. You can hire and fire all staff (scouts, medical, etc.), scout deep into any league you include (more on this later), set specific practice routines with the coaches you hire for specific players or your team as a whole, set specific tactics for each line, set tactics down to the specific player ie. if they carry the puck, if they have shoot/pass tendency, et cetera, and a very fleshed out drafting system and player development system which can seem entirely predictable until your #1 pick goes full Nail Yakupov. And there is much, much more.

The beauty of this game, to me, is that it's very customizable. You can add leagues, teams, players, mostly anything you want to do if you wish to invest the time in it. The steam workshop has plenty of add-ons, including rosters, facepacks, team logos, some of which I would argue are almost mandatory. Some might call this a knock on the game but it is not licensed, so while you don't get all of the logos and player's faces by default, it's easily added later. I personally roll with all of the facepacks and logos, as I feel it adds to the experience of the game and there's no negative. This part is entirely up to you, you could roll with default everything including roster, if you wanted to. There's generally current rosters in the workshop as well.

There are a couple negative factors to this game but they are rather minor. I had some crashing issues with a specific roster I had downloaded which likely stemmed more from the roster and less from the game. If I were to check the stats of some staff, the game would freeze. Not entirely too awful as long as you have an autosave, but annoying nonetheless. I've never had this problem with TBL roster, which could almost be considered the "official" roster update. Beyond that, the game -can- run slow if you turn on too many options or don't change the detail level. For example, if you use the largest database, and have more then one league on full detail, it will take quite a while to sim a day. In my experience, if you change the detail levels and use only one league, it sims quite quickly. Not a huge deal. Beyond that, I guess the only other thing I can think of is the learning curve. At first it's very steep, and you might find yourself a little overloaded, but if you persevere it's very rewarding and deep.

All in all, I'd highly recommend this game if you're passionate about hockey, or even if you just enjoy sports sims. As the game says, "there's a lot to like here".

if you play the GM mode in EA Sports NHL series and are disappointed year after year with the lack of depth and challenge, this could be what you're looking for.

there are a couple of hurdles right off the hop that can turn off a new player, but if you get passed them, you should be on your way to a rewarding (and time devouring) experience.

first hurdle is the lack of official licenses (except for, i think, EIHL & EPHL [U.K.]), but this is easily overcome with community made databases and picture/logo packs either from the steam workshop or from ehmtheblueline.  

second hurdle is the menu navigation.  they have improved it somewhat from when the game was in early access, but given how deep the game can be, i think the menus are about as simple as they can make them.  all i can say for this is just stick with it, you'll figure out where everything is eventually.


the challenges and depth EHM offers over EAs NHL GM modes is, in my opinion, like night and day.  admittedly, i haven't touched EAs NHL series since NHL14, but i'm guessing the GM modes haven't really been touched since then.  the biggest differences i can name off the top of my head are:

the closest you can get to the ice is coaching, you cannot jump onto the ice during the third period and single handedly overcome a 4 goal deficit.  that doesn't mean that your team can't do it, you just can't do it for them.  this definitely ups the challenge since you can't cheese your way to the playoffs or a cup with a no chemistry bottom feeder team.

there are no solid concrete "overall" or "potential" ratings.  there are skill ratings and statistics for you to scour over and determine how they're developing and if/where they will fit into your roster.  you also have scouts, trainers, coaches, and assistant GM that will give you a fair idea of how good a player is or their potential, but like real world, they can sometimes be very wrong.  i've had players that all my staff said were going to be a first line talent or starting goalie go completely bust, and i've had players that staff said had 4th line or no potential turn out consistent 50+ point seasons.

i also find trading and free agency to be far more difficult.  there are no interest meters for free agents and they may sign with another team for more than they requested when you offered.  sometimes your UFAs want to test out free agency, or just don't want to play for you anymore.  sometimes your foreign prospects wont be willing to leave their countries or teams.  you're also unlikely to be the clear cut immediate winner in a trade, especially if you're the one proposing it and the player you're offering for isn't on the trading block.  trading up 1:1 for a slightly better player is rare and you're not going to get to Crosby, Kane, Stamkos, Karlsson, Price, etc. this way.

anyway, i think that covers most of the important stuff and i'm getting sick of typing.  if you want something deeper than EAs NHL GM modes and are willing/determined enough to get passed the initial hurdles, there's a potentially very addicting game that awaits... just look at my play time.

There is so much that I could go on about regarding this game, but I'll try to keep this as short and as sweet as possible. This game is as close to the ideal hockey management sim there has ever been, by a long shot, and that can probably be seen in my hours played lol. The amount of detail and customization available in this game is staggering, and the ability to pick any league/team is refreshing, as taking over junior teams is one of my favourite features. The drafting/scouting system is very well thought out, and even acts like real life, with players falling/rising and teams drafting based on positional needs rather than BPA. Free agency can be a little iffy at points, with many core/superstar players all available at once. The salary cap rises very slowly from year to year, which is another issue, but it's a fun challenge to go along with building a dynasty. Developing prospects requires patience and playing them in the right spots, and it really is rewarding to develop a superstar, or watch a 6th round pick grow into a key player. Trading is good as well, as there will be times where you get 'ripped off' and others where you come off with a steal - asset management is a big thing in this game. The only complaints I have, albeit minor, is that if you draft well, the game gets easy very quickly, as you just trade good players for picks, let them develop, and repeat. As well, if you don't know hockey that well, the game may be a bit tricky to begin with, but the tutorials help with that. Additionally, the custom roster/logo//facepacks that come along with the game are very well done. I would highly recommend this to any hockey fan/sports management fan - 10/10, 2 thumbs up!

I supported this title expecting the same level of dedication to quality was one finds in Football Manager (not that FM is without it's issues - but it is a very good game); but this - EHM, is not anything like its sports management brother. 

This game is apparently a product from developed back in 2007. And it looks like it. Important features are buried behind menus and different screens and navigating to them is far from intuitive. So your left blindly clicking hoping to find what you need. To make matters worth, some buttons are links without a hover state. So it doesn't look like a button or link, and doesn't behave like one until clicked. I discovered some features this way be accident. You can filter some lists, but I've always found this buggy. 

Then there's how data is laid out, which is in a busy, packed manner. Wheres FM lays things out in easy to look at, well spaced datas, organized in a pleasing and logical layout; in EHM you have glaring or just poorly chosen colors that either flash or blend with the games background. And did I mention that to date you're going to play this in windowed mode in a display resolution harkoning back pre-1080p monitors? Yes. This game doesn't know what 16:9 is.

The actual games are laid out on a 2d, with stick-figure hockey sticks glued to little circles. Albeit this is better than OOTPs rendition, but its a laugh-out-loud insult to those who enjoy the live 3d action of FM.

I could go on, but, to end on a positive is the community. There are update rosters and all kinds of nuggets of info to be found at http://www.ehmtheblueline.com/forums/portal.php.

To be fair, to date I've put in 10hrs and aside from the horrific UI - when you get the hang of it I did have fun. But I just find the interfaces learning curve to much work that it sucks all the joy out of what could be a really fun game.

A very flexible game that let's you be the General Manager for a team at almost any level of hockey. You manage coaching staff, scouts, players and contracts. You can coach at a very detailed level or leave those details to the AI. Many features will let you play your way.

Even though the game has a lengthy manual, much of how it works it not explained. This is one of those games that you need to figure out and google. You will learn about hockey and how it works. You will learn about how hockey works and how this game is different.

I learned the game and the many options. While I found it acceptable, I also find it falls short in some important design areas.

For example, [url=community.sigames.com/showthread.php/456266-April-2016-r-EHM-priotized-enhancments]here[/url] is a long list of possible enhancements for the latest version 1.1. You can see in this discussion that the developer is not aligned with the reality of their game (regarding salary cap). This shows a lack of thorough design.

When I first bought the game at version 1.0.2, it would frequently lock up. There was a work-around where you could "go on vacation" to get past the day with the error but you were then missing the simulation for that day. I'm a lifelong Football Manager player, but IRL my main love is hockey. I've been waiting for a FM-type game for hockey to come out for as long as I can remember, but after playing so much FM, none of these hockey sims can even come close. It's absurd how far ahead FM is of ANY NHL or NFL sim games. Here is what EHM needs to fix before I'll be interested in playing again:

-Interface: I can't use touchscreen or keyboard arrows to navigate. Here's an example of why that sucks. I offer a player I want to trade around to the league. I get 10 offers in return. In order to dismiss them all (because all the offers are laughably awful, I just need to know which teams are interested), I have to click the message in my inbox (middle of my screen), then mouse all the way down to the bottom to "cancel offer", then mouse back up to the next message, then back down the bottom, etc. Why can't I use "arrow down", "hotkey to dismiss", "arrow down", "hotkey to dismiss"? Why isn't there even an option to set a hotkey to dismiss? Stuff like this is LITTERED throughout the game. After you've gotten used to the wonderful menus and interface in Football Manager, this game looks like it was made by a 3rd grader. In FM you can sort ANY chart you're looking at by any column. This would be SO useful to have. Want to compare career goals over the last 3 years for a handful of forwards you're considering? Too bad, you can't.

-Trading: The AI cannot properly value draft picks. If you offer five 1st rounders for a 3rd line winger, the AI will refuse. I spent hours trying to get a team to trade me a 1st line winger, and even when I match up their "wants" exactly they tell me to go fuck myself. I'm not trying to make a team of Connor McDavids, I just want  to add a Bryan Rust-calibre player and it's literally impossible no matter what assets I send in return. Also, your fans and board always get pissed at you for any trade you make, even if its getting Ovechkin for Cody Ceci (tho I'm sure Ottawa would reject that trade in this game).

That's my entire list. Fix the interface, make trading work. EHM already has my other necessary requirement for a hockey sim - a functional 2D match engine that actually shows the gameplay. I cannot stand text-based games. The sad thing is, this is the best hockey management sim out there. FHM is even worse. But as it is, I do not enjoy playing EHM and will not be recommending it.

This game is so full of bugs it's stupid and what's worse is that the developer has seemingly abandoned the game altogether. When I first downloaded the game about a year ago everything was great. The dev released very frequent updates and bug fixes and everything was peachy. The game ran super fast and smoothly and while there were small problems there was nothing major that had a big effect on gameplay. 

These frequent updates continued until the game was finally released until December 1st, 2015, when the game was taken out of Early Access and given a full release. As a huge fan of the game I was super excited for this new "EHM 1". There were a lot of cool new features added and it was the biggest update I had seen thus far. Unfortunately EHM 1 would be the beginning of the steep decline in the quality of EHM. This 1.0 update was so full of bugs it was actually unplayable for a large portion of players. Myself and a ton of other users had to spend days combing online forums and google searches for solutions to the problems we faced. I remember being so frustrated that this huge update came out on December 1st but I actually couldn't play it until mid December, and even then I just kept playing a save game from an earlier version of the game because the new version was so messy.

As if this disaster of an update wasn't bad enough, a lot of these bugs have gone totally unfixed even now on May 29th, 2016. Since the 12/1 full release, there have been only 3 updates to the game, the last coming out more than 3 months ago on February 17th. These updates were two minor bug fix updates and then a 1.1.1 update that added some new content to the game. The game is still in shambles, and the developer hasn't touched the game in more than 3 months. He used to release updates on a weekly basis, and now he doesn't release updates at all.

Let me break down a couple of the major bugs that have made me want to pull my hair out, and keep in mind that this isn't all of them.

- You can't minimize this game. If you minimize the game, or if some pop-up automatically minimizes the game you can't open the game back up. You better hope that you saved recently because all of your progress will be lost. This bug has been around since the December 1st update, and has been unsolved for almost 6 months now.

- The in-game clock was completely ruined by the December 1st update. In EHM you can't play the games, you just simulate all of them. You can mess with the in-game clock settings to make it slow, medium, or fast. I can't speak for everyone, but my friends and I and a lot of other people I've seen on the online forums play the game on the fastest clock settings. We do this because we don't want to sit and watch a simulated game for a long period of time, we'd rather it just be over with as fast as possible. Before the December 1st update you could simulate a game in under 30 seconds and it was absoulutely tremendous. Being able to fly through games so fast meant that you could finish entire seasons relatively quickly and your manager's career would progress at a nice pace. The December 1st update made the clock much much slower than it was before, even on the fastest settings. That quick 20 second game suddenly took almost a minute or more to simulate. I get that a 50 second game still doesn't seem like much, but when all you can do is just sit there and watch a screen for 50 seconds you get bored really quickly. This bug actually frustrated me to the point where I just stopped playing the game completely for almost a month. It's a really boring game when you have to stare at your screen for a collective two hours and do nothing just to finish one season. Luckily I found a fix to that bug by tinkering with the settings, and I was able to play the game with a super fast clock again, until earlier today. My clock is now super slow again, and there is NOTHING I can do about it. I've already tinkered with the settings as much as I can and my clock is super slow. I'm sick about it.

- The bug I talked about earlier that kept most players from playing the new update for a few days after the 1.0 release is still around for a lot of new players. Whenever you start up the game you get some error message that breaks the game. You can't open the game, you can't do anything until you go into the game's properties and change all of the resolution settings, just so you can finally open the game and change the in-game resolution settings, before you go back and reset your computer's resolution settings. You have to do all of this annoying tinkering just to be able to play the game! Come on Riz!

This game is super fun, don't get me wrong. I've played more than 400 hours. Unfortunately this is a game I cannot recommend to anyone, as it is just a giant headache.

I'm sure the developer Riz is working on other games, and I'm sure he's very busy. He's the only developer of this game and while I'm very thankful for all of the work he's done the fact of the matter is that this game is abandoned right now. There hasn't been an update in MONTHS, not even a tiny bug fix!! I don't understand why the guy would just let this game that he worked so hard on sit and rot.

TL:DR
This game right now is a buggy pile of mush. Before it was taken out of early access it was absoulutely brilliant, but now that it has been fully released it has been completely abandoned by the developer. Only buy this game if you want to deal with a bunch of problems before you can really enjoy the game. Don't buy this game unless it's on sale.
